cards.front: Recall a key point about The Golden Years: Stresemann
cards.back: Gustav Stresemann served as Chancellor for just 102 days (August-November 1923) but remained Foreign Secretary from August 1923 until his death on 3 October 1929. He was the dominant figure in German politics during the "Golden Years" and was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926 alongside French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Golden Years: Stresemann
cards.back: The Dawes Plan, negotiated by American banker Charles Dawes, restructured Germany's reparations payments. Annual payments were reduced from £50 million to a starting figure of £10 million, rising to £25 million over 5 years. Crucially, it also arranged American loans of 800 million gold marks to Germany.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Golden Years: Stresemann
cards.back: The Locarno Pact was signed on 16 October 1925 in Locarno, Switzerland. Germany, France and Belgium agreed to guarantee their mutual western borders as set by Versailles. This was hailed as the beginning of a new era of peace - the "Locarno Spring" or "Locarno Honeymoon."

cards.front: Recall a key point about The Golden Years: Stresemann
cards.back: The Weimar Republic (1919-1933) was one of the most creative periods in German cultural history. Berlin became one of the most exciting and cosmopolitan cities in Europe, known for its art, cinema, architecture, and nightlife.

cards.front: What should you know about key judgement?
cards.back: The "Golden Years" were golden mainly for the urban middle class and big business. Farmers, agricultural workers, and those on fixed incomes continued to struggle. The recovery was built on fragile foundations - American loans that could be withdrawn at any time. When the Wall Street Crash happened in October 1929, just a month after Stresemann's death, the entire recovery collapsed.

cards.front: What does New Objectivity (Neue Sachlichkeit) mean?
cards.back: Artists like Otto Dix and George Grosz painted harsh, realistic images of Weimar society - wounded veterans, prostitutes, corrupt businessmen
